summary: Most files in this batch are in good shape: gemini schema sanitizer is well-tested, gemini-types are an honest wire-shape mirror, the Codex OAuth flow has a credential-redacting Debug impl, probe.rs is documented as a single source of truth, and model_override_provider.rs carries incident-history comments on each non-obvious choice. Two Medium findings warrant fixing: Ollama error mapping ignores HTTP status codes, and the Codex browser-flow leaks its fixed callback port on caller cancellation. Two Low findings: a duplicated default-token-lifetime fallback and a stale docstring example.

findings.title: OllamaProvider::handle_error never classifies HTTP status codes
findings.description: handle_error inspects response.status() but only uses it for a log line and the fallback message. The only structured case it special-cases is `error_msg contains "model" && contains "not found"` (good — surfaces a missing-model in the user-actionable form). Every other 4xx/5xx — including 401 (auth header rejected), 403 (forbidden), 429 (rate limit) and 503 (server overloaded, common while a large model is loading into memory) — funnels into `AlephError::provider(...)`. Callers that classify errors for retry/backoff (`failover/`, the harness retry layer, the gateway RPC's transient-vs-permanent split) cannot tell an Ollama "still loading" 503 from a payload-validation 400, so transient failures may not be retried and permanent ones may be retried indefinitely. A 401 is also returned to the user as a generic provider error rather than as the credential problem it actually is.

findings.title: authorize_via_browser leaks the localhost:1455 callback server on caller cancellation
findings.description: authorize_via_browser spawns the axum callback server bound to the hard-coded CALLBACK_PORT (1455, mandated by OpenAI's redirect_uri) into a tokio task (`server_handle`, line 301), then aborts that handle ONLY in explicit early-return paths (lines 314, 324, 328, 335, 344) or after success. If the caller's future is dropped between the spawn and any of those abort calls — e.g., the gateway handler times out, the user navigates away in the desktop shell, or the supervising task is cancelled while waiting for the user to complete the browser dance — there is no abort. The detached axum task keeps listening on 1455 indefinitely (or until process exit), so every subsequent Codex login attempt fails at the `TcpListener::bind` step with "Failed to bind localhost:1455 — is another login in progress?". The `Failed to open browser` path is correctly aborted (and even has a comment explaining why), so the fix pattern is already known to the author; it just needs to extend to the cancellation case.

findings.title: expires_in.unwrap_or(3600) fallback duplicated in exchange and refresh
findings.description: Both `exchange_code_for_token` (line 388: `let expires_in = token_resp.expires_in.unwrap_or(3600);`) and `refresh` (line 449: identical line) silently fall back to a 3600-second lifetime if the server omits `expires_in`. The value is duplicated, magic, and the two sites can drift apart if one is ever changed. There is no `tracing::warn!` to surface that the server's normal response shape is missing the field, so a server-side bug (e.g., dropping `expires_in` from the JSON envelope) would be invisible until tokens started failing mid-flight.

findings.title: MockProvider docstring example uses the pre-Removed process signature
findings.description: The module-level docstring (`src/providers/mock.rs:38-90`) contains a `rust,ignore` example that calls `provider.process("input", None).await.unwrap()` and compares the result directly to a `&str`. The current `AiProvider::process` signature takes `RequestPayload<'_>` and returns `ProviderResponse`; the live usage pattern (used by every test in the same module, e.g. line 175, 200, 213) is `provider.process(RequestPayload::new(&msgs)).await.unwrap()` then `response.text_content()`. Because the example is marked `rust,ignore` rustdoc does not compile it, so the docs build is green — but a new user copy-pasting from these docs gets a hard signature mismatch and has to reverse-engineer the real one from the tests or the trait definition. The example also claims `provider.process("input", None).await` returns the response, when the current method returns `Result<ProviderResponse>`.
